title: The five-level network model for ML training
question: How do physical links become a usable training fabric?
scope: The five tiers organize dependent design concerns; the upward arrow denotes abstraction, not a measured performance gain.

steps.title: Move bits
steps.description: L1 starts with SerDes signaling and the copper or optical path. Every higher-level transfer must first cross these physical links.

steps.title: Transfer between accelerators
steps.description: L2 adds RDMA, RoCEv2, and GPUDirect to connect GPU memory through NICs. Its cost includes both startup latency and payload transfer.

steps.title: Arrange available paths
steps.description: L3 connects switches into a topology. The arrangement determines which paths and shared cuts carry simultaneous collective traffic.

steps.title: Handle competing traffic
steps.description: L4 governs queues, congestion feedback, and routing under load. A connected topology alone does not establish good collective completion time.

steps.title: Integrate the cluster
steps.description: L5 combines the lower tiers with placement and failure domains. A production training fabric must satisfy all five levels together.

title: Historical network bandwidth scaling
question: What does the historical link-rate gap tell us about crossing a node boundary?
scope: The series compare per-direction link budgets, including summed NVLink links per GPU and individual external ports. They are product specifications, not collective timings.

steps.title: Use a common unit
steps.description: The vertical axis is per-direction bandwidth on a logarithmic scale. Equal vertical distances represent equal ratios rather than equal absolute rate increases.

steps.title: Locate the local budget
steps.description: NVLink appears in 2016 and rises above the external-port series. Its points represent the GPU’s aggregate intra-node budget in the charted configurations.

steps.title: Compare the exit path
steps.description: Ethernet and InfiniBand external ports offer smaller budgets than NVLink in these configurations. Crossing nodes can therefore expose a narrower communication path.

steps.title: Avoid a timing shortcut
steps.description: The shaded gap bounds a resource mismatch. Payload size, port provisioning, routing, contention, and overlap determine how much of it a training step actually experiences.

title: The bandwidth hierarchy
question: Which hierarchy boundary creates the bandwidth cliff?
scope: These are per-direction budgets across four specified generations. Comparing one external port with aggregate GPU NVLink bandwidth does not predict achieved collective bandwidth.

steps.title: Separate the storage and links
steps.description: The legend distinguishes on-package HBM, intra-node NVLink, one InfiniBand port, and the PCIe host bus. These resources serve different parts of a data path.

steps.title: Read the H100 cliff
steps.description: The H100 annotation compares NVLink with one NDR InfiniBand port, showing about a ninefold per-direction budget gap. It is not a ratio of measured training times.

steps.title: Compare generations consistently
steps.description: V100 and A100 show roughly twelvefold gaps in the same comparison, while B200 shows eighteenfold. Improvements within the node do not automatically remove its external-port bottleneck.

steps.title: Place frequent exchanges carefully
steps.description: A partition with frequent per-layer exchanges benefits from remaining inside the higher-bandwidth domain when feasible. Workload dependencies and provisioning still decide the actual cost.

title: The bandwidth cliff in a training step
question: Where does exposed communication lengthen a training step?
scope: The 1 ms and 30 ms AllReduce durations are illustrative assumptions; the percentages are compute shares of these schedules, not measured GPU utilization.

steps.title: Hold computation fixed
steps.description: Both rows contain 100 ms forward and 100 ms backward phases. The shared axis makes their equal compute budgets visible.

steps.title: Add a short synchronization
steps.description: The intra-node row adds the assumed 1 ms AllReduce after backward computation. Compute occupies 99.5 percent of this illustrative step.

steps.title: Expose the longer transfer
steps.description: The inter-node row waits another 30 ms before the next dependent work can begin. With no overlap in the drawing, compute occupies 87 percent of the step.

steps.title: Interpret the gap
steps.description: The wider red interval explains the lower compute share. It is a schedule comparison, not a transfer-time prediction from the network bandwidth ratio.

title: From NRZ to PAM4 signaling
question: Why can PAM4 carry more bits per symbol while reducing voltage margin?
scope: Equal symbol periods and normalized voltage ranges are a schematic comparison, not a complete link throughput or error-rate model.

steps.title: Encode one bit
steps.description: The NRZ panel uses two signal levels. Its six symbol slots encode six bits.

steps.title: Encode a pair
steps.description: PAM4 selects among four levels for each symbol. The same six symbol slots encode twelve bits.

steps.title: Pay for closer levels
steps.description: The PAM4 level spacing is one third of the full swing. Distinguishing nearby levels demands greater signal integrity and error-control care.

steps.title: Separate encoding from delivered rate
steps.description: The panel compares bits per symbol; coding overhead and link implementation still determine usable bandwidth and latency.

title: GPUDirect RDMA data path
question: Which host-memory staging traffic does GPUDirect RDMA avoid?
scope: The diagram isolates the sending-node path. Direct GPU-memory access still uses the platform interconnect and does not eliminate all CPU setup or network costs.

steps.title: Locate the payload
steps.description: The payload n starts in GPU memory. The RDMA NIC must obtain those same bytes before sending them to the fabric.

steps.title: Trace host staging
steps.description: The dashed route stages the payload through registered host memory. Its write and reread account for approximately 2n bytes of staging-bus traffic.

steps.title: Follow direct DMA
steps.description: The green GPUDirect route connects GPU memory to the RDMA NIC through the PCIe fabric. It avoids the illustrated host-memory staging round trip.

steps.title: Keep the boundary explicit
steps.description: Avoiding host staging does not remove the NIC, PCIe path, or external fabric. Their bandwidth and topology still constrain the transfer.

title: Traditional TCP/IP vs. RDMA verbs stacks
question: What changes when transport moves from sockets to RDMA verbs?
scope: The two panels contrast representative data paths. RDMA bypasses the kernel in the steady-state data path, not in every setup and control operation.

steps.title: Start with sockets
steps.description: The left framework sends from a host-memory buffer through the Socket API. The drawn buffer chain includes two CPU-mediated copies.

steps.title: Execute transport in software
steps.description: The kernel TCP/IP stack performs reliability and the NIC driver fills its transmit ring before DMA. These operations occupy the left data path.

steps.title: Post work with verbs
steps.description: On the right, NCCL posts work through the verbs API. The data path then proceeds to the RDMA NIC without traversing the kernel transport stack.

steps.title: Read accelerator memory
steps.description: The green connection marks the NIC reading GPU memory directly through GPUDirect. RDMA transport offload and direct accelerator access are distinct parts of this path.

title: The $\MessageStartupLatency$-$\LinkBandwidth$ crossover
question: Where does transfer startup stop dominating payload transmission?
scope: Both curves are alpha + n/beta scenarios. Their parameter values describe the declared paths and do not establish universal protocol latency or bandwidth.

steps.title: Pay startup for a small message
steps.description: At the left, reducing payload size barely changes total time. Startup alpha dominates both nearly flat curves.

steps.title: Balance the two terms
steps.description: A crossover occurs where alpha equals n/beta. The marked knees differ because each path has a different startup and bandwidth pair.

steps.title: Read the asymptotes
steps.description: The dotted InfiniBand startup floor and transmission line meet below its actual curve. At equality, total time includes both terms rather than equaling either alone.

steps.title: Grow the payload
steps.description: Far to the right, n/beta dominates and total time rises nearly proportionally with message size. End-to-end measurements are still needed to locate a real path’s crossover.

title: Measured All-Reduce Time against the Two-Parameter Model
question: Where does a two-parameter AllReduce model explain the measurements, and where does it miss?
scope: The red points are one eight-H100 NVLink NCCL run. NVLink SHARP status is unspecified; this inspection cannot attribute residual error to one unmeasured mechanism.

steps.title: Distinguish observations from model
steps.description: The red markers are measured times and the solid line is the two-parameter model. Both axes are logarithmic, so gaps are relative differences.

steps.title: Fit the small-message floor

steps.title: Inspect the middle mismatch
steps.description: Around the knee and through intermediate message sizes, measured points sit above the model. Matching the endpoints does not guarantee an accurate transition region.

steps.title: Check the bandwidth end
steps.description: The largest-message delivered bandwidth anchors the other end, where line and measurements converge. This is a useful bound model rather than a complete explanation of all collective regimes.

title: Non-blocking fat-tree topology
question: How do leaf, spine, and core paths connect GPUs across pods?
scope: This is the printed small topology with four core, eight spine, eight leaf switches and sixteen endpoints; its connectivity alone is not a universal bandwidth guarantee.

steps.title: Enter at the leaf
steps.description: Each GPU endpoint enters the fabric through its leaf switch. Dashed pod boundaries group the leaf and spine resources.

steps.title: Use multiple upward paths
steps.description: Leaves connect to the spine tier rather than relying on a single uplink. These alternate paths distribute cross-pod traffic when routing and provisioning permit.

steps.title: Cross the core
steps.description: The highlighted route climbs through a core switch and descends into a different pod. A cross-pod transfer consumes resources at multiple tiers.

steps.title: Check provisioning
steps.description: The right margin lists switches, endpoints, and links by tier. Nonblocking behavior requires suitable link capacities and routing, not merely a tree-shaped drawing.

title: Rail-optimized physical wiring
question: Why connect the same GPU position to a dedicated network rail?
scope: The drawing shows four rails and three nodes as a schematic subset; the spine is explicitly not drawn, and rail locality depends on the job partition.

steps.title: Retain fast local exchange
steps.description: Each node has GPU 0 through GPU 3 joined by its own NVSwitch. Tensor-parallel work can remain within this local domain.

steps.title: Connect matching positions
steps.description: The cabling joins the same GPU position across nodes to the corresponding rail switch. These are same-position paths rather than one shared switch for every GPU.

steps.title: Match the parallel split
steps.description: A data-parallel group that holds the same shard at matching GPU positions can use its dedicated rail. Other traffic patterns may require the bridging fabric.

steps.title: Do not hide upper tiers
steps.description: The upward note says the spine is not drawn. The lesson identifies locality, not a claim that every transfer avoids spine capacity or contention.

title: An illustrative bandwidth-cost scenario for ML network topologies
question: Why is topology choice a comparison of a declared configuration rather than a family name?
scope: Bandwidths follow the stated structures and link rate; costs are assumed scenario inputs. The dashed trend is a visual comparison, not a universal pricing law.

steps.title: Read both axes
steps.description: Moving right buys more bisection bandwidth; moving up pays more assumed cost per Gb/s. The torus point has the smallest capacity and lowest assumed price in this scenario.

steps.title: Compare the configured alternatives
steps.description: The rail-optimized and fat-tree points offer more cut capacity at higher assumed unit cost. Their coordinates belong to these particular structures and provisioning choices.

steps.title: Inspect the exception
steps.description: The tapered dragonfly sits above the drawn price-capacity trend. Its long-link savings at larger scale need not appear at the scenario’s cluster size.

steps.title: Retain the scenario boundary
steps.description: Changing endpoint count, radix, routing, link speed, or equipment price can move these points. A topology family name alone does not establish the plotted ranking.

title: A PFC deadlock from a cyclic buffer dependency
question: Why can four full queues remain blocked after traffic injection stops?
scope: A directed cycle alone is insufficient: this example additionally assumes occupied buffers, blocked successors, and persistent PAUSE states.

steps.title: Need downstream space
steps.description: Switch 1 holds packets whose next buffer is b2. The solid clockwise arrows continue this requirement through b3 and b4 back to b1.

steps.title: Pause the predecessor
steps.description: Each full queue sends PAUSE upstream, against the forwarding direction. Switch 2 therefore prevents its predecessor from sending more traffic.

steps.title: Close the waiting cycle
steps.description: All four queues wait for successors that are themselves blocked. No queue can drain enough to clear its PAUSE state.

steps.title: Break a dependency
steps.description: In the depicted deadlock, stopping new injection is insufficient. Recovery must break the closed wait, for example through the stated watchdog dropping packets.

title: A true incast burst
question: Why does this incast overflow one egress despite fast sender links?
scope: This is the chapter’s deliberately worst-case fan-in, not a bandwidth-optimal ring AllReduce or a measured arrival trace.

steps.title: Aggregate arrivals
steps.description: The senders each offer 50 GB/s toward the same destination. The placeholder stands for 252 additional senders, so this is a many-to-one burst.

steps.title: Identify the narrow exit
steps.description: The single 400 Gb/s egress serves 50 GB/s. It cannot drain bytes as fast as this assumed fan-in supplies them.

steps.title: Fill a finite queue
steps.description: The switch buffer absorbs the difference only temporarily. Once its 32 MB capacity is exhausted, the system must drop packets or reduce arrivals.

steps.title: Move pressure upstream
steps.description: The red PAUSE path shows backpressure returning toward senders. It can prevent a local drop while spreading blocked traffic through shared upstream resources.

title: Iron law diagnostic flowchart
question: Which bottleneck should be diagnosed before choosing a kernel optimization?
scope: The flow is a troubleshooting guide, not a proof that a utilization threshold uniquely identifies the limiting resource.

steps.title: Start outside the kernel
steps.description: A missed target with low accelerator utilization first calls for stall diagnosis. An accelerator waiting for input cannot benefit from faster arithmetic alone.

steps.title: Eliminate feeding overhead
steps.description: The right branch checks I/O, CPU preprocessing, and exposed communication. Each branch names a different intervention because each delays useful device work differently.

steps.title: Classify busy execution
steps.description: Once the device is usefully occupied, compare arithmetic intensity with the ridge point. Below the ridge the bandwidth bound is tighter; above it the compute bound is tighter.

steps.title: Choose and verify a remedy
steps.description: Memory-bound remedies reduce traffic or improve reuse; compute-bound remedies reduce arithmetic cost or active work. Re-profile because removing one bottleneck can expose another.

title: The roofline model
question: Which ideal resource bound limits each operation at its stated intensity?
scope: Markers lie on ideal FP16 bounds for the declared H100 configuration; they are not measured kernel throughput. Arithmetic intensity uses bytes crossing the stated memory boundary.

ridge.label: Ridge at about 295 FLOP per byte

ceiling.label: FP16 compute ceiling and high-intensity markers

steps.title: Bound traffic-limited work
steps.description: The blue slope multiplies arithmetic intensity by HBM bandwidth. Batch-one decode lies far left because little arithmetic is performed per byte of weights moved.

steps.title: Increase data reuse
steps.description: Unfused attention prefill also lies on the slope in the stated workload. Reducing HBM traffic can raise its intensity without requiring the same proportional increase in arithmetic.

steps.title: Find the binding-resource switch
steps.description: At the ridge, the HBM bound meets the FP16 compute ceiling. The tighter ideal bound changes from memory bandwidth to compute capacity.

steps.title: Interpret the upper markers
steps.description: Tiled attention prefill and the large GEMM reach the ideal ceiling at their plotted intensities. Actual implementations can remain below it because scheduling, locality, or other overheads intervene.

title: The profiling hierarchy
question: How does profiling connect a fleet symptom to a hardware cause?
scope: The windows illustrate narrowing diagnostic scope; their trace shapes are schematic rather than a measured common execution.

steps.title: Find the service symptom
steps.description: The application trace compares behavior against the SLO over fleet-hours. Its highlighted window selects the interval worth investigating.

steps.title: Locate the slow rank or operation
steps.description: Framework and distributed traces narrow the scope to ranks and steps. The marked straggler is evidence about where the symptom concentrates.

steps.title: Inspect execution gaps
steps.description: The kernel timeline resolves stream activity in milliseconds. Launch gaps and communication overlap become visible at this scale.

steps.title: Test a hardware explanation
steps.description: SM-level counters expose bandwidth, occupancy, and stalls over microseconds. This detail can explain a kernel cause but must remain connected to the original application symptom.

title: Operator fusion before and after
question: Which activation transfers disappear when these operators fuse?
scope: The figure counts activation transfers only; weights and small vectors are omitted, and equal transfer counts need not mean equal byte counts.

steps.title: Read the unfused path
steps.description: Linear, GELU, and LayerNorm execute as separate kernels. The path reads X and writes Y, and also writes and rereads both intermediates.

steps.title: Materialize the middle values
steps.description: Z1 and Z2 cross the HBM boundary between their producers and consumers. These four intermediate transfers are the red paths.

steps.title: Keep intermediates on chip
steps.description: In the fused kernel, the same operator sequence passes Z1 and Z2 on chip. The dashed HBM boxes explicitly show that those intermediates are not materialized there.

steps.title: Interpret the saving
steps.description: Only the activation read of X and write of Y remain at the drawn HBM boundary. This is a traffic mechanism, not a proportional speedup guarantee.

title: FlashAttention memory hierarchy tiling
question: How does FlashAttention avoid storing the full score matrix in HBM?
scope: The drawn tile schedule explains storage placement. SRAM capacity, accumulators, buffering, and tile reloads still affect the complete working set and traffic.

hbm.label: HBM matrices Q, K, V, O

tiles.label: Loaded Q, K, V tiles in SRAM

steps.title: Stage blocks
steps.description: The selected Qi, Kj, and Vj tiles are loaded from HBM to SRAM. The full input and output matrices remain in HBM.

steps.title: Consume a score tile
steps.description: The on-chip product Sij = Qi Kj transpose produces one score tile. It is consumed locally instead of becoming a full sequence-by-sequence HBM tensor.

steps.title: Update normalization online
steps.description: Running maxima and sums let softmax incorporate successive tiles. The output accumulator is rescaled as the normalization changes.

steps.title: Write the accumulated output
steps.description: After the required tiles have been processed, Oi is written to HBM. Eliminating the quadratic intermediate does not eliminate input loads or tile reloads.

title: FlashAttention memory savings
question: Why does eliminating the quadratic attention workspace matter more at long context?
scope: The chart counts resident attention workspace for 32 FP16 heads. Its ratios are capacity comparisons, not HBM traffic ratios, total-model memory, or speedup.

steps.title: Store the full scores
steps.description: The red standard-attention curve grows quadratically with sequence length because the full score matrix is resident in HBM.

steps.title: Keep running statistics
steps.description: The blue FlashAttention curve grows linearly in this workspace accounting. Online softmax avoids materializing the full quadratic score matrix.

steps.title: Compare at a fixed context
steps.description: At 8K tokens, the vertical comparison spans the two workspace requirements and is labeled 4,096 times smaller. This is a capacity ratio at one sequence length.

steps.title: Extend context without changing the metric
steps.description: At 64K the plotted ratio grows to 32,768. The freed capacity can support KV cache, activations, or batches, but the ratio is not a runtime prediction.

title: Block-wise versus per-tensor quantization
question: How does block scaling confine an outlier’s quantization damage?
scope: This fixed eight-weight INT8 example demonstrates representation resolution; it is not a model-quality or kernel-speed benchmark.

steps.title: Find the extreme value
steps.description: Both panels contain the same weight 58.7 beside much smaller values. One tensor-wide scale must accommodate that outlier.

steps.title: Lose small-value resolution
steps.description: With the shared coarse scale, six small weights round to zero and the remaining small weight rounds to one. INT8 range is spent representing the outlier.

steps.title: Separate the blocks
steps.description: The right panel assigns one scale to each four-weight block. The block without the outlier can use a much finer scale.

steps.title: Confine rather than erase damage
steps.description: The first block retains distinct integer values; small weights sharing the outlier’s block still collapse. More blocks require more scale metadata.

title: Deep learning compilation pipeline
question: How do four captured operations become three generated kernels?
scope: This is one illustrative lowering of a feed-forward block; backend decisions and actual kernel counts depend on the model and target.

steps.title: Capture the operations
steps.description: TorchDynamo records Linear, GELU, Linear, and LayerNorm. The captured graph contains four operations.

steps.title: Expose GEMM primitives
steps.description: Graph-level decomposition and optimization represent the linear stages as GEMM plus bias. Operation identity is retained while the compiler exposes lower-level structure.

steps.title: Form a fused group
steps.description: TorchInductor groups the first GEMM with its GELU epilogue. The remaining GEMM and LayerNorm stay separate, giving three groups.

steps.title: Select executable kernels
steps.description: Code generation maps the fused group and normalization to Triton and the separate GEMM to cuBLAS in this example. The result is three kernels, not a universal compiler promise.

title: Speculative decoding process

steps.title: Propose a short future

steps.title: Verify the prefix together
steps.description: One target pass checks the proposed positions. The illustrated acceptance test accepts T1 through T3 and rejects T4.

title: The overlap budget
question: Why can a fixed compute budget hide a shrinking share of communication?
scope: The normalized bar values are illustrative operating points. GPU count alone does not determine overhead, and overlapped time is not an extra serial cost.

steps.title: Keep computation fixed
steps.description: The dashed line holds useful computation at 100 units. Violet overlap occupies time inside that budget rather than being added serially on top.

steps.title: Inspect the small case
steps.description: At the smallest scale, little communication remains above the compute budget. Most of its assumed communication can fit behind independent computation.

steps.title: Exhaust the hiding window
steps.description: At larger scales, the red hatched portion extends far above the same compute budget. That exposed portion lengthens the modeled execution window.

steps.title: Read the denominator correctly

steps.description: The early points rise from the A11’s 0.6 TOPS rating. These are stated peak capability indicators rather than measured application throughput.

steps.title: Separate derived evidence
steps.description: A13 uses a hollow marker because its value is derived from stated speedups. Its evidence differs from a directly stated rating.

title: On-device prediction strategies
question: How do next-word suggestions differ from inline Smart Compose?
scope: The screenshots show request-time local inference. They do not depict a federated-training round or show how shared model parameters are updated.

steps.title: Condition on typed context
steps.description: The left input reads “What’s your”. Next-word prediction uses that local context to rank discrete candidate tokens.

steps.title: Offer separate candidates
steps.description: “favorite,” “address,” and “schedule” appear in a suggestion bar. Selecting a candidate is a request-time interaction with the inference output.

steps.title: Complete inside the buffer

steps.title: Keep inference separate from training

title: Local-only, centralized-cloud, and federated learning
question: What crosses the device boundary in each learning architecture?
scope: The three panels are alternatives, not stages in a required evolution. Keeping raw data local does not by itself protect model updates or metadata.

steps.title: Train without exchange
steps.description: Panel A keeps training on the device and sends nothing across the dashed boundary. There is no server contribution in this local-only architecture.

steps.title: Upload raw examples
steps.description: Panel B moves device data to the cloud trainer. The server sees the raw examples that drive centralized training.

steps.title: Exchange model state
steps.description: Panel C downloads the global model theta and uploads changes delta theta. Raw data stays on the device while model state crosses the boundary.

steps.title: Separate locality from privacy
steps.description: The federated path changes what leaves the device; it does not establish that the update reveals nothing about local data. Updates and metadata still require explicit privacy controls.

title: The training memory amplifier
question: Which additional objects amplify the memory cost of training?
scope: The example assumes FP32 weights, Adam state, and activations fixed at five times weight memory. Its ninefold ratio is representative for this configuration, not a universal training multiplier.

steps.title: Begin with resident weights
steps.description: The inference bar contains 40 MB of weights for the 10M-parameter FP32 example. Training retains those weights as well.

steps.title: Add parameter-dependent state
steps.description: Gradients add another 40 MB and Adam state adds 80 MB. These objects must be distinguished from the original weights when budgeting memory.

steps.title: Include saved activations
steps.description: The assumed 200 MB activation region is the largest part of the training bar. The complete example reaches 360 MB rather than the 40 MB inference footprint.

steps.title: Retain the stated assumption
steps.description: The right panel keeps the same ninefold total ratio across model sizes because the accounting assumptions scale together. Real activation lifetimes and optimizer choices can change that ratio.

title: Adaptation memory budget
question: What must fit in working memory before local adaptation can run?
scope: Segment heights are schematic. The peak is taken over the actual live activation-plus-workspace sum, not a sum of independently occurring peaks.

steps.title: Distinguish storage from residency
steps.description: Frozen weights in flash occupy deployment storage. Once staged into SRAM or RAM, resident weights and staging workspace count against working memory.

steps.title: Add trainable state
steps.description: Gradients and optimizer state for the selected trainable parameters occupy a separate region. Freezing weights can reduce this region without removing the resident base.

steps.title: Follow the live peak
steps.description: Activations and operator workspace change during execution. The drawn peak must reflect their simultaneous live sum under the actual schedule.

steps.title: Reserve room for the device
steps.description: Admission requires the adaptation peak plus the runtime and foreground-app reserve to fit under the device limit. The dashed red ceiling represents that complete constraint.

title: The edge inference landscape
question: Why are edge latency-energy points not a matched-workload efficiency ranking?
scope: Published points use different inference tasks and acceleration paths. Tier shading is descriptive; the chart does not compare training performance or directly determine battery life.

steps.title: Locate small-task devices
steps.description: The MCU/ASIC region includes keyword spotting, visual wake words, and small-image tasks. Their energy and latency points describe the specific published workloads.

steps.title: Compare the higher tiers carefully
steps.description: Coral and Jetson points operate at larger energy scales; the Jetson label explicitly names ResNet-50. Moving between tiers also changes the workload.

steps.title: Qualify the apparent gap
steps.description: The roughly hundredfold energy separation mixes hardware efficiency with task size. It cannot establish that one platform is that much more efficient on the same task.

steps.title: Budget repeated operation
steps.description: Energy per inference is one input to a device budget. Training frequency, inference frequency, sensing, radio use, and idle power are additional costs outside this plot.

title: TinyTL adaptation paths
question: Why can TinyTL reduce memory without shortening the backward path?
scope: The diagram compares update structure and retained state; actual savings depend on activation, normalization, and residual-module choices.

fullstate.label: Full-path retained state and backward pass

tinyblocks.label: Frozen TinyTL blocks and trainable biases

tinystate.label: TinyTL backward state and full-depth arrow

steps.title: Update every weight
steps.description: Full fine-tuning trains the backbone and classifier. The left state columns represent dependencies retained or recomputed for those gradients.

steps.title: Restrict trainable parameters
steps.description: TinyTL freezes the main block weights while training biases, lite residual modules, and the classifier. Gray backbone weights remain present in the model.

steps.title: Keep backward reach
steps.description: The dashed backward arrow still spans the TinyTL network. Gradients must traverse frozen blocks to reach trainable biases at earlier depths.

steps.title: Explain the memory lever
steps.description: TinyTL changes which backward values must remain live rather than simply stopping backpropagation early. Activation and normalization choices determine the remaining state.

title: LoRA architecture
question: Which LoRA parameters train, and what can be merged for serving?
scope: The diagram uses one square base matrix. Merging requires a supported numerical representation, and trainable-parameter savings are not total-model memory savings.

steps.title: Retain the base computation
steps.description: The input x follows the frozen W0 path. Frozen means no base parameter gradients or optimizer state, not that the base weights disappear.

steps.title: Learn a low-rank correction
steps.description: A maps the input down to rank r, then B projects back to dimension d. Only these two matrices are trainable in the drawn update.

steps.title: Add the two outputs
steps.description: The summation forms h = W0 x + BA x. The adapter changes the layer output while retaining the frozen base contribution.

steps.title: Consider a merged representation
steps.description: For supported serving formats, BA can be folded into W0 to form one matrix. Compatibility, requantization, and any retained copies still affect deployment cost.

title: Selective on-device fine-tuning
question: How is a device budget turned into a selective fine-tuning plan?
scope: Benefit scores and the cut are schematic. Independently ranked layer gains and costs need joint validation when selected units train together.

ranking.label: Benefit per unit device cost ranking

steps.title: Prepare an adaptable base
steps.description: The cloud stage meta-trains the full network on generic data so that later local updates can adapt it. This is distinct from the subsequent device-specific selection.

steps.title: Rank candidate units
steps.description: Layers or channel groups are ordered by expected adaptation benefit per unit of device cost. The horizontal axis accumulates device cost.

steps.title: Apply the measured budget
steps.description: The red cut limits what fits the device’s data, compute, and memory allowance. A high-ranked unit still needs a feasible combined execution schedule.

steps.title: Train only the selected set
steps.description: The final panel updates Layer 3 and the head while freezing other units in this schematic case. Backward dependencies through frozen layers may still incur work and storage.

title: Federated averaging protocol
question: Which client updates actually enter one FedAvg round?
scope: The diagram uses example-weighted aggregation of completed clients. It does not claim this objective is universally fair or that all invited clients finish.

steps.title: Invite and initialize
steps.description: The coordinator selects a cohort and broadcasts the round’s global model. Selection policy determines which population gets a chance to contribute.

steps.title: Compute on private data
steps.description: Each client runs local epochs on its own dataset. The unequal timeline lengths show that completion times need not match.

steps.title: Enforce the deadline
steps.description: Only completed uploads enter this round. Client 5 crosses the red deadline and is dropped, so its examples are absent from the round denominator.

steps.title: Weight the completed models
steps.description: The coordinator averages completed client models with weights based on their local example counts. A user-weighted objective would require a different declared aggregation rule.

title: Measuring the local-work trade-off
question: Why do fewer federated rounds not always mean less wall-clock time?
scope: These timelines illustrate opposing effects of local work, not measured convergence curves or a universally best epoch count.

steps.title: Count both kinds of time
steps.description: Blue intervals are local epochs and orange intervals are upload and synchronization. A round includes both, so communication frequency alone does not determine completion time.

steps.title: Amortize synchronization
steps.description: The moderate setting does more local work per round and reaches its target with fewer rounds in this schematic example. Its endpoint lies earlier on the shared wall-clock axis.

steps.title: Account for client drift
steps.description: The large setting lengthens rounds and includes the hatched round added by drift. Fewer synchronizations can still produce a later target endpoint.

steps.title: Measure time to target
steps.description: Compare the row endpoints only after checking quality, total client energy, and population coverage. The diagram supplies a comparison method, not an admissible policy by itself.

title: Communication-computation trade-off in federated learning
question: Why does a slower network move the toy model’s preferred local-work setting?
scope: The curves are an illustrative relative-cost model rather than measured convergence results. Their minima require later validation of drift, energy, and client coverage.

steps.title: Amortize expensive exchange
steps.description: At very little local work, repeated synchronization dominates the model, especially for the slow network. Increasing local epochs initially reduces that cost.

steps.title: Locate the fast-network minimum
steps.description: The dotted fast-network curve reaches its minimum at ten epochs. With cheap exchange, less local work is needed to amortize communication.

steps.title: Move under slower communication
steps.description: The medium and slow curves place minima at twenty and forty epochs. The arrow summarizes this shift under the declared cost model.

steps.title: Stop before local work dominates
steps.description: The curves eventually rise because additional local work carries cost and stands in for growing drift penalties. These toy minima do not replace deployment measurements.

title: Gradient compression techniques
question: What changes besides payload size when an update is compressed?
scope: The four-coordinate illustration excludes full protocol overhead. Quantization needs scale metadata, and sparsification needs indices and persistent residual storage.

steps.title: Transmit full precision
steps.description: Panel A sends all four 32-bit values. The payload bar shows 128 value bits before protocol metadata.

steps.title: Quantize every coordinate
steps.description: Panel B represents all coordinates with INT8 values. Its 32 value bits require a scale, and the reconstructed values generally have quantization error.

steps.title: Send selected coordinates
steps.description: Panel C transmits the two selected values along with their coordinate identities. Values alone would not tell the receiver where to apply them.

steps.title: Retain omitted information
steps.description: The residual stays on the client for error feedback into later updates. Compression saves transmitted bytes while creating local state that must fit the device budget.

title: Federated personalization architectures
question: How does the adaptation choice change backward-state requirements?
scope: The comparison fixes the shown backbone structure. Frozen parameters remove their own gradients and optimizer state, but not every backward dependency.

steps.title: Train the whole network
steps.description: Full fine-tuning updates each layer and the task head. The full-height backward arrow and hatched state column show its deep backward dependencies.

steps.title: Stop at the head
steps.description: Head-only adaptation freezes the feature extractor. In this comparison, backpropagation stops at the task head, so the backbone’s backward state is unnecessary.

steps.title: Train small modules at depth
steps.description: Adapters leave backbone weights frozen but introduce trainable modules beside its layers. Reaching those modules requires backward propagation through the intervening frozen backbone.

steps.title: Separate parameters from live state
steps.description: Small trainable parameter count alone does not establish a short backward path. The hatched marks identify state that must still be retained or recomputed.

title: Secure aggregation protocol
question: How can the server recover a sum without seeing each raw update?
scope: This two-client illustration assumes both complete and do not disclose their masks. It demonstrates cancellation, not dropout recovery, collusion resistance, or differential privacy.

a.label: Client A adds the shared mask

b.label: Client B subtracts the shared mask

steps.title: Agree on one shared mask
steps.description: Clients A and B share the random mask s. The server does not receive s as an ordinary upload in this illustration.

steps.title: Mask opposite contributions
steps.description: Client A forms yA = delta theta A + s, while Client B forms yB = delta theta B − s. Each transmitted vector hides its individual raw update under the stated assumptions.

steps.title: Upload masked values
steps.description: Only the orange masked vectors cross into the aggregation-server domain. Conventional per-client inspection of the raw contributions is therefore unavailable.

steps.title: Cancel in the sum
steps.description: Adding yA and yB cancels +s and −s, leaving the exact aggregate of both updates. The aggregate can still reveal information and may need differential privacy.

title: Measured AI Performance across Phone Processors
question: Why can one local-work quota fail across a heterogeneous phone fleet?
scope: AI Benchmark scores measure inference through each processor’s software acceleration path. Release year and family do not isolate hardware causality or predict training speed.

steps.title: Read a measured score
steps.description: The plot combines processor release years with logarithmic AI Benchmark inference scores. The colors identify processor families, not controlled experimental conditions.

steps.title: Keep older devices in the fleet
steps.description: The shaded 2020-onward window still contains much lower-scoring processors than the leaders. A current fleet can contain widely different execution paths and capabilities.

steps.title: Inspect the full within-window range
steps.description: High-scoring recent processors extend the range upward. The right bracket shows roughly a four-hundredfold score spread within the shaded window.

steps.title: Schedule with measured device budgets
steps.description: A single local-work quota may not fit this population. Training feasibility must still be measured because these inference scores do not establish backward speed or memory capacity.

title: Tiered adaptation strategy
question: How should adaptation demand and device limits guide deployment?
scope: The cards describe candidate adaptation methods, not rigid device tiers. Every branch still requires measured quality, memory, runtime, and energy feasibility.

steps.title: Ask what change is needed
steps.description: A light adaptation need routes toward bias-only updates. A powerful device does not make a larger update necessary if the smaller method meets the quality target.

steps.title: Admit a larger candidate
steps.description: A heavier change requires checking whether the larger update fits compute and energy limits. The moderate adapter branch remains a candidate when full fine-tuning is unnecessary or infeasible.

steps.title: Check whether sharing helps
steps.description: Only after selecting an adaptation candidate does the flow ask whether updates are valuable across devices. This determines whether federation is useful.

steps.title: Choose an operational policy
steps.description: Local-only deployment uses local validation and monitoring; federation adds coordination and appropriate privacy controls. The named differential-privacy configuration is not mandatory for every threat model.

title: Edge MLOps lifecycle pipeline
question: How does an adapted device model remain part of a managed release lifecycle?
scope: The pipeline distinguishes raw-data locality from privacy of returned telemetry. A retraining trigger is a decision requiring validated evidence, not proof of regression.

fleet.label: First, wider, and pending rollout waves

steps.title: Prepare tier-compatible releases
steps.description: Cloud pretraining produces the base model, and compression creates forms suited to different device tiers. Compatibility includes the permitted local update policy.

steps.title: Roll out in stages
steps.description: The over-the-air stage releases to a first wave before a wider wave. Not-yet-updated devices coexist with newer versions.

steps.title: Adapt under the policy
steps.description: The device keeps local data and adapts the permitted model components. Versioned weights alone no longer describe every behavior that can emerge.

steps.title: Return governed evidence
steps.description: Telemetry supplies aggregate metrics through privacy controls. Keeping raw data local does not make those returned metrics inherently private.

steps.title: Validate before retraining
steps.description: The dashed feedback path can trigger cloud retraining when the evidence warrants it. A detected change must first be distinguished from an actual quality regression.

title: On-device shadow validation
question: Why is prediction disagreement a gate rather than a verdict?
scope: The comparator is label-free. A threshold crossing signals change but does not identify which model is correct or prove a quality regression.

models.label: Shared inputs and two prediction rows

steps.title: Compare on the same inputs
steps.description: The frozen baseline and serving candidate receive x1 through x8. Their class predictions differ at x4 and x7 in this example.

steps.title: Measure a label-free change
steps.description: The comparator marks equality or disagreement without ground-truth labels. It cannot tell which disagreeing prediction is correct.

steps.title: Hold on a threshold crossing
steps.description: The disagreement-rate bar exceeds tau and feeds the gate. The gate suspends the candidate rather than declaring a regression.

steps.title: Decide using validated evidence
steps.description: A validated outcome signal or safety invariant supports the final decision. Clear returns the candidate to service; confirmed regression justifies rollback.

title: The Fleet Stack Revisited
question: Where do the six fleet principles apply in the stack?
scope: The arrow indicates scale-induced change across all bands and is not a seventh principle. Responsibility and sustainability divide governance by obligation.

steps.title: Start with capability
steps.description: Infrastructure owns Facility and Accelerators together with Fabric and Storage. FLOP/s, bandwidth, and rack power constrain what the fleet can execute.

steps.title: Separate execution from recovery
steps.description: Distribution contains communication can dominate and failure is routine as distinct row-level principles. Exposed communication time and recovery overhead answer different questions.

steps.title: Keep the serving contract
steps.description: The Serving territory covers runtime, serving, and operations. Its p99-within-SLO metric evaluates delivered service rather than raw token rate alone.

steps.title: Distinguish governance obligations
steps.description: Responsibility covers Assurance and the governance half of the top row. Sustainability occupies the resource half with energy-per-query and carbon metrics.

steps.title: Read the scale premise
steps.description: The vertical arrow spans every band because scale changes the behavior of the whole stack. It connects the six territories without adding another principle.

title: From Model Serving to Closed-Loop Agentic Fleets
question: Why must an agentic workflow be measured per verified result?
scope: The panels illustrate accounting boundaries, not measured energy or a guarantee that additional verification improves quality at acceptable cost.

steps.title: Count a model token
steps.description: Panel a encloses one model forward pass. FLOPs per token and joules per token describe cost within that narrow execution boundary.

steps.title: Expand to the complete task
steps.description: Panel b includes planning, retrieval, tool execution, and verification. Model calls are components inside this workflow rather than the whole unit of work.

steps.title: Charge retries to the task
steps.description: A failed verification returns the workflow to planning. Work spent on failed attempts remains part of the cost of the eventual useful result.

steps.title: Use a verified output unit
steps.description: The final accounting unit is the useful task completed at the required quality and safety. A cheaper token does not by itself establish a cheaper successful workflow.

title: The queuing hockey stick
question: Why does retaining utilization headroom matter in an M/M/1 queue?
scope: The curve is mean system occupancy L = rho/(1 − rho) for a stable M/M/1 queue, including the request in service. The shaded thresholds are illustrative, not universal safe limits.

steps.title: Identify what is counted
steps.description: L counts requests in the system, including any request currently being served. The equation describes occupancy rather than latency in milliseconds.

steps.title: Leave room to drain bursts
steps.description: At lower utilization the expected occupancy grows gradually. Spare service capacity gives a stable system more opportunity to drain accumulated work.

steps.title: Observe nonlinear growth
steps.description: At rho = 0.8 the displayed equation gives L = 4. Increasing utilization further raises occupancy rapidly rather than adding a constant penalty.

steps.title: Approach the stability boundary
steps.description: The curve diverges as rho approaches one from below. The colored operating bands illustrate headroom choices and must not be read as universal production thresholds.

title: Batch Size Trade-Off Curves
question: Why can larger batches improve throughput while taking longer to finish?
scope: The dimensionless toy model is t(B) = 1 + 0.15(B − 1), with throughput B/t(B). It excludes queuing and batch formation, and asserts no optimal batch or memory limit.

steps.title: Establish the reference
steps.description: At batch one, both normalized quantities equal one. The curves compare relative throughput and relative batch completion time rather than raw units.

steps.title: Amortize fixed work
steps.description: As batch size grows, B/t(B) rises with diminishing returns. Multiple examples share the fixed component of the assumed service cost.

steps.title: Pay longer service time
steps.description: The red t(B) curve continues increasing while throughput begins to level. Higher throughput can therefore coexist with a longer wait for a complete batch execution.

steps.title: Do not select an optimum from the crossing
steps.description: The two normalized curves use different quantities. Their crossing is not an optimal batch size, a latency SLO, or a memory-capacity boundary.
